newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan Phosphate tops $350 mln revenue in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Jordan Phosphate tops $350 mln revenue in 1996.

text.p: Jordan Phosphate Mines Company announced on Thursday its revenues grew nine percent in 1996 to $350 million, driven higher by healthy world demand.

Majority state-owned JPMC, Jordan's sole phosphate producer and one of the world's largest phosphate suppliers, also said major joint ventures with Indian and Japanese firms would start up in 1997 as it diversified into downstream operations.

"There was an increase in the export revenue of Jordan Phosphate Mines Company (JPMC) by $30 million with the value of exports reaching $350 million in 1996," Sameh al-Madani, the general manager of the company, said in a statement.
Earnings this year were boosted by a higher quantity of sales to West European markets, Australia and New Zealand along with traditional Asian sales and buoyant rock phosphate prices.
Exports of raw phosphates rose 12.2 percent to 4.35 million tonnes in 1996 from 3.878 million tonnes in 1995.

An additional 1,114,5009 tonnes were used by the firm's major fertiliser complex in the Red Sea port of Aqaba, which produces mainly di-ammonium phosphate, whose value-added exports rose 3.2 percent in 1996 to 712,000 tonnes, Madani said.
Madani said the company would see in 1997 its first two major fertiliser joint ventures with foreign partners come on stream .
The $170 million Indo-Jordan Chemicals, which will export phosphoric acid to a fertilizer complex in India, was on target to start production by mid-1997, Madani said.
The plant, close to Aqaba industrial complex, will use 750,000 to 800,000 tonnes of raw phosphates a year from the nearby Shidiyah plant in southern Jordan.
Annual sales are expected to be $70-$80 million dollars.

Indo-Jordan Chemicals is Jordan's largest fertilizer joint venture. India's Southern Petrochemical Industries Corporation (SPIC) has a 52.2 percent equity share, JPMC a 34.8 percent stake while the Riyadh-based Pan Arab Investment Company has an 13 percent share. It will produce 220,000 tonnes annually of phosphoric acid for a major SPIC fertiliser complex.
Jordan is India's major supplier of phosphate rock for its fast growing fertiliser industry. India imports between 1.2-1.5 million tonnes annually of phosphate rock.

The second joint-venture is the $85 million Nippon-Jordan Chemical Company, a joint venture with the Arab Potash Company and a Japanese consortium. Its 300,000 tonne a year compound fertiliser and ammonium phosphates plant in Aqaba is due for completion in the first quarter of 1997, Madani said.

Jordan Phosphate Mines had also completed feasibility studies for an estimated $250 million second stage expansion of the Shidiyah mine which would more than double production to around eight million tonnes by 1998, Madani said.
The first stage, costing an estimated $180 million, is expected to increase production to 3.25 million tonnes by the end of 1997.
"This important project will allow us to double raw phosphates from Shidiyah and so enable it to cover the needs of the joint projects and international markets," Madani said.
Shidiyah mine, with high grade phosphate, is by far the lowest cost producer of Jordan's three operating mines. It holds one billion of Jordan's 1.5 billion tonnes of proven reserves.
Negotiations were still going on with Norway's Norsk Hydro on a possible fertiliser complex to produce 500,000 tonnes annually of phosphoric acid, company officials.
